subtopic_detail: a rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge that worsened after surgical debridement
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 44-year-old woman on the surgical ward. A small pustule on her left shin three weeks ago broke down into an ulcer, and she was taken to theatre for debridement eight days ago because it was thought to be infected. The wound has enlarged from 3 cm to 9 cm since the operation.

On examination the ulcer has a deep necrotic base with a raised violaceous overhanging border and a surrounding rim of erythema, and the skin at the edges of the surgical incision has itself broken down. Pedal pulses are easily palpable and the ankle brachial index is 1.05 bilaterally. Two wound swabs and two sets of blood cultures have grown no organisms despite eight days of intravenous flucloxacillin, and a punch biopsy from the edge shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no organisms on special stains and no vasculitis. She has had intermittent bloody diarrhoea for two years that she has not sought help for. Her temperature is 37.2 degrees Celsius, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) and C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Wound examination: 9 cm ulcer with necrotic base, raised violaceous overhanging border, breakdown at the surgical incision edges
data_table.Vascular assessment: Easily palpable pedal pulses, ankle brachial index 1.05 bilaterally
data_table.Microbiology: Two wound swabs and two sets of blood cultures with no growth after eight days of intravenous flucloxacillin
data_table.Histology: Dense neutrophilic infiltrate, no organisms on special stains, no vasculitis
data_table.Other history: Two years of intermittent bloody diarrhoea, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and repeat the wound swab in two days
options.rationale: She has already completed eight days of exactly this treatment with sterile cultures and a deteriorating wound, and the biopsy shows no organisms on special stains. Repeating a failed antimicrobial strategy delays the immunosuppression that will stop the ulcer extending. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply negative pressure wound therapy and continue regular sharp debridement
options.rationale: Negative pressure therapy has a role once the disease is immunologically controlled, but combining it with ongoing sharp debridement continues the mechanical trauma that drives pathergy. It is the near pair to reasonable wound care, and the distinguishing point is that the timing relative to immunosuppression is what makes it helpful or harmful. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Refer for arterial duplex imaging and consideration of revascularisation
options.rationale: An arterial ulcer is a legitimate differential for a necrotic leg ulcer but is excluded by easily palpable pedal pulses and a normal ankle brachial index. Arterial ulcers also have a punched-out rather than undermined violaceous border. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Leg ulcers)

options.text: Start systemic corticosteroid therapy and avoid any further debridement
options.rationale: Enlargement of the ulcer after surgery and breakdown at the incision edges is pathergy, which with a violaceous undermined border, sterile cultures and a neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy indicates pyoderma gangrenosum. High dose systemic corticosteroid with strict avoidance of further surgical trauma is first-line treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Arrange a further wider debridement with split skin grafting to follow it
options.rationale: Surgery is the single most harmful intervention in this condition because pathergy causes the wound to extend along every new incision, which is exactly what has already happened. Grafting without immunosuppression reliably fails and creates a second pathergic wound at the donor site. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

explanation.summary: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis rather than an infection, despite a name that has misled clinicians for a century, and it typically begins as a pustule or nodule that breaks down into a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border. It is a diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test, so infection, vasculitis, malignancy, venous and arterial disease and calciphylaxis are ruled out by culture, biopsy and vascular assessment before it is accepted. Around half of cases are associated with a systemic disease, most often inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder, and the undisclosed bloody diarrhoea here points to an underlying colitis that needs investigation in its own right. Pathergy, in which minor trauma provokes new or extending lesions, is the feature that makes the condition dangerous in surgical hands, because each debridement enlarges the wound and the deterioration is then misread as worsening infection prompting yet more surgery. Treatment is immunosuppression, beginning with high dose systemic corticosteroid or ciclosporin, with tumour necrosis factor inhibitors used for refractory disease or where inflammatory bowel disease coexists, alongside meticulous non-traumatic wound care and adequate analgesia.
key_points: Pathergy means the ulcer extends after surgery, which is often misread as infection.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; biopsy shows neutrophils and excludes other causes.
Around half of cases have an associated systemic disease, often inflammatory bowel disease.
Treatment is systemic immunosuppression with strict avoidance of further debridement.
explanation.pearls: A leg ulcer that gets dramatically bigger in the days after debridement, with sterile cultures despite adequate antibiotics, is pyoderma gangrenosum until proven otherwise, and the next operation will make it worse rather than better.
